title: Human Nutrition and Digestion
description: The components of a balanced diet and the deficiency diseases scurvy and rickets, the organs of the alimentary canal and their functions, physical and chemical digestion with the key enzymes, and absorption in the small intestine for IGCSE Biology 0610.

notes.heading: The Balanced Diet (7.1.1)
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A **balanced diet** contains **all the essential nutrients in the correct proportions**, together with enough energy for the person's needs.

🔑 The components the 0610 syllabus names
• **Carbohydrates** and **fats/oils** — energy.
• **Proteins** — growth and repair.
• **Vitamins C and D** and the mineral ions **calcium** and **iron** — small amounts, specific jobs.
• **Fibre** and **water** — no energy, but essential.

🔑 What the examiner wants
'Balanced' means the right PROPORTIONS matched to the person — age, activity and health all change what is balanced. A diet can contain every nutrient and still be unbalanced if the proportions are wrong.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Listing foods instead of nutrients, or saying a balanced diet 'contains no fat'. Fats are essential — it is the proportions that matter.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Balanced diet = all nutrients + fibre + water, in correct proportions.
• Only carbohydrates, fats and proteins provide energy.

notes.heading: Carbohydrates, Fats and Proteins: Sources and Importance (7.1.2)
notes.body:
You must state the **principal sources** and the **importance** of each named nutrient.

🔑 Carbohydrates
• Sources: bread, rice, pasta, potatoes, sugar.
• Importance: the main source of **energy** — digested to glucose, which cells respire.

🔑 Fats and oils
• Sources: butter, cooking oils, cheese, oily fish, nuts.
• Importance: a concentrated **energy store**, and a layer of fat under the skin **insulates** the body.

🔑 Proteins
• Sources: meat, fish, eggs, beans, nuts.
• Importance: **growth and repair** of tissues — proteins supply the amino acids used to build new cells, enzymes and muscle.

💡 Worked Example
'Suggest why a growing teenager needs more protein than an elderly person.' Answer frame: protein provides amino acids for growth and repair; the teenager is building new tissue, so their demand is higher.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'protein gives you energy' as its main role. It can be respired, but its named importance at Core is growth and repair — give that answer first.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Learn each nutrient as source + importance, in that pair.
• Carbs and fats = energy; protein = growth and repair.

notes.heading: Vitamins C and D, Calcium, Iron, Fibre and Water (7.1.2–7.1.3)
notes.body:
🔑 The remaining components
• **Vitamin C** — sources: citrus fruits, peppers, green vegetables. Importance: healthy skin and gums, wound healing. **Deficiency causes scurvy** — bleeding gums and wounds that heal slowly.
• **Vitamin D** — sources: oily fish, eggs; also made in skin exposed to sunlight. Importance: helps the body absorb **calcium** for bones and teeth. **Deficiency causes rickets** — soft bones that bend and deform.
• **Calcium** — sources: milk, cheese, leafy green vegetables. Importance: making and maintaining **bones and teeth**.
• **Iron** — sources: red meat, spinach, lentils. Importance: making **haemoglobin**, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
• **Fibre** — sources: wholegrain cereals, fruit and vegetables. Importance: gives the gut muscles bulk to push against, keeping food moving and preventing **constipation**.
• **Water** — sources: drinks and food. Importance: the **solvent** for the body's chemistry and for transport in the blood.

🔑 The deficiency pair to learn cold
**Scurvy = lack of vitamin C. Rickets = lack of vitamin D (or calcium).** Both are named explicitly on the Core syllabus, so a one-mark 'name the deficiency disease' question is guaranteed marks if you know the pair.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Swapping scurvy and rickets. Anchor it: scurvy → Sailors → Citrus (vitamin C); rickets → bones → vitamin D helps absorb calcium.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Vitamins and minerals give no energy but are essential in small amounts.
• Scurvy = vitamin C; rickets = vitamin D/calcium; iron → haemoglobin; fibre → gut movement; water → solvent.

notes.heading: The Alimentary Canal and Its Associated Organs (7.2.1)
notes.body:
🔑 The canal in order — food passes through these
**mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine (duodenum, then ileum) → large intestine (colon, then rectum) → anus**
Learn the small intestine in its two parts — **duodenum** (first part, where the pancreas and liver deliver their secretions) and **ileum** (where absorption happens) — and the large intestine as **colon**, **rectum** and **anus**.

🔑 The associated organs — food does NOT pass through these
• **Salivary glands** — secrete saliva (containing amylase) into the mouth.
• **Pancreas** — secretes digestive enzymes into the duodenum.
• **Liver** — connected to the gut by the bile duct.
• **Gall bladder** — a small sac tucked under the liver that stores the liver's secretion and releases it into the duodenum.

🔑 What the examiner wants
Identification questions show a diagram and ask you to label or name organs — so know the POSITIONS, not just the list: salivary glands by the mouth, stomach as a J-shaped sac below the oesophagus, the coiled small intestine framed by the wider large intestine, liver above the stomach with the gall bladder beneath it, pancreas in the loop of the duodenum.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Routing food through the liver or pancreas. Associated organs only SECRETE into the canal — the tube itself is mouth to anus.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Canal: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → duodenum → ileum → colon → rectum → anus.
• Associated: salivary glands, pancreas, liver, gall bladder.

illustration.alt: Labelled diagram of the human alimentary canal — mouth, oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, ileum, colon, rectum and anus — with the associated organs: salivary glands, liver, gall bladder and pancreas.
illustration.caption: Food travels only through the canal itself; the salivary glands, pancreas, liver and gall bladder are associated organs that secrete into it.

notes.heading: Ingestion to Egestion: the Five Processes (7.2.2, 7.5)
notes.body:
📌 The five definitions — quote them exactly
• **Ingestion** — taking substances (food and drink) into the body through the mouth.
• **Digestion** — the breakdown of food into smaller pieces (physical) and into small soluble molecules (chemical).
• **Absorption** — the movement of small soluble food molecules and ions from the small intestine into the blood.
• **Assimilation** — the absorbed molecules move into cells and are USED, becoming part of the cells — e.g. glucose used in respiration, amino acids built into the body's own proteins.
• **Egestion** — the removal of undigested food from the body as faeces, through the anus.

🔑 Where absorption happens (7.5.1–7.5.2)
The **small intestine is the region where absorption takes place** — digested food molecules pass into the blood here. **Most water is also absorbed in the small intestine**, with **some water absorbed in the colon** on the way to the rectum.

🔑 Absorption vs assimilation — the classic discrimination
Absorption gets the molecule OUT of the gut and INTO the blood. Assimilation is what the CELLS do with it afterwards. If a question asks what happens to glucose 'after it is absorbed', the answer is assimilation.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing egestion with excretion. Faeces were never absorbed into the body's cells — egestion simply removes undigested material. Do not call it excretion.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Five processes in order: ingest → digest → absorb → assimilate → egest.
• Absorption (and most water uptake) = small intestine; some water = colon.

notes.heading: Physical Digestion and Teeth (7.3.1–7.3.6)
notes.body:
📌 Definition
**Physical digestion** is the breakdown of food into **smaller pieces without any chemical change** to the molecules.

🔑 Why it matters
Smaller pieces have a much **larger surface area**, so the enzymes of chemical digestion can act on the food **faster**. No new substances are made — that is what separates it from chemical digestion.

🔑 The four types of teeth and their functions
• **Incisors** — flat, chisel-shaped front teeth for **biting and cutting** food.
• **Canines** — pointed teeth for **gripping and tearing**.
• **Premolars and molars** — broad, ridged back teeth for **chewing and grinding**.

🔑 Tooth structure — label every layer
• **Enamel** — the hard, non-living outer layer protecting the crown.
• **Dentine** — the softer, bone-like layer beneath the enamel.
• **Pulp** — the soft centre containing the **nerves and blood vessels**.
• **Cement** — anchors the root of the tooth in the jawbone.

🔑 Churning
Physical digestion is not only teeth: the muscular wall of the **stomach churns** the food, mixing it with the stomach's juices and breaking it into smaller pieces.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying physical digestion 'breaks down molecules'. It only breaks PIECES of food into smaller pieces — the molecules themselves are unchanged.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Physical = smaller pieces, more surface area, no chemical change.
• Incisors cut, canines tear, premolars/molars grind; enamel → dentine → pulp (nerves + blood vessels) → cement.

notes.heading: Chemical Digestion: the Enzymes and Hydrochloric Acid (7.4.1–7.4.5)
notes.body:
📌 Definition
**Chemical digestion** is the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into **small, soluble molecules** by **enzymes**, so that they can be **absorbed** into the blood.

🔑 The three enzymes — what, where secreted, where it acts, product
• **Amylase** — secreted by the **salivary glands** and the **pancreas**; acts in the **mouth** and the **small intestine**; breaks **starch** down into **simple reducing sugars**.
• **Protease** — secreted by the **stomach** and the **pancreas**; acts in the **stomach** and the **small intestine**; breaks **proteins** down into **amino acids**.
• **Lipase** — secreted by the **pancreas**; acts in the **small intestine**; breaks **fats and oils** down into **fatty acids and glycerol**.

🔑 Hydrochloric acid in the stomach (7.4.5) — TWO functions, both needed for the marks
1. It **kills microorganisms** swallowed with the food.
2. It provides the **acidic pH** that the stomach's enzymes need for **optimum activity**.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Two frequent slips: saying amylase 'makes glucose' (the Core statement is simple reducing sugars), and crediting the stomach with lipase (lipase acts only in the small intestine). The details of bile and the named proteases pepsin and trypsin are Supplement material, not required for this topic.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Amylase: starch → reducing sugars (mouth + small intestine).
• Protease: protein → amino acids (stomach + small intestine).
• Lipase: fats → fatty acids + glycerol (small intestine only).
• HCl: kills microorganisms + acidic pH for stomach enzymes.

flashcards.definition: A diet containing all the essential nutrients in the correct proportions, with enough energy for the person's needs.
flashcards.example: Plenty of fruit and vegetables, starchy carbohydrates for energy, some protein and dairy, and only small amounts of fat and sugar.

flashcards.definition: The deficiency disease caused by a lack of vitamin C — bleeding gums and poor wound healing.
flashcards.example: Prevented by eating citrus fruits and fresh vegetables.

flashcards.definition: The deficiency disease caused by a lack of vitamin D (or calcium) — soft bones that bend and deform.
flashcards.example: Vitamin D from oily fish, eggs and sunlight lets the body absorb calcium for hardening bones.

flashcards.definition: Taking substances into the body through the mouth.
flashcards.example: Eating a sandwich is ingestion; what the gut does next is digestion.

flashcards.definition: The movement of small, soluble food molecules and ions from the small intestine into the blood.
flashcards.example: Amino acids from digested protein are absorbed in the ileum.

flashcards.definition: Absorbed molecules moving into cells and being used, becoming part of the cells.
flashcards.example: Glucose used in respiration and amino acids built into muscle protein are both assimilation.

flashcards.definition: The removal of undigested food from the body as faeces, through the anus.
flashcards.example: Dietary fibre is never digested or absorbed, so it is egested.

flashcards.definition: The breakdown of food into smaller pieces without chemical change, increasing the surface area for enzymes to act on.
flashcards.example: Chewing with the teeth and churning by the stomach wall.

flashcards.definition: Enzyme that breaks starch down into simple reducing sugars; secreted by the salivary glands and pancreas, acting in the mouth and small intestine.
flashcards.example: Crackers begin to taste sweet if chewed for a long time as salivary amylase releases sugars.

flashcards.definition: Enzyme that breaks proteins down into amino acids; secreted by the stomach and pancreas, acting in the stomach and small intestine.
flashcards.example: Stomach protease works best in the acidic pH provided by hydrochloric acid.

flashcards.definition: Enzyme that breaks fats and oils down into fatty acids and glycerol; secreted by the pancreas and acting in the small intestine.
flashcards.example: Cream is digested to fatty acids and glycerol in the duodenum and ileum.

flashcards.definition: Acid secreted by the stomach wall; kills microorganisms in food and provides the acidic pH for optimum enzyme activity.
flashcards.example: Without it, stomach protease works poorly and more harmful bacteria survive.

questions.stem: Which foods are principal sources of protein?
questions.explanation: Protein comes from meat, fish, eggs, beans and nuts. Butter and oils are fat sources, citrus fruits supply vitamin C, and wholemeal bread is mainly carbohydrate and fibre.

questions.stem: Scurvy is caused by a lack of which nutrient?
questions.explanation: Scurvy — bleeding gums and poor healing — results from vitamin C deficiency. Lack of vitamin D (or calcium) causes rickets, and lack of iron causes anaemia.

questions.stem: A child has soft bones that are starting to bend. Which deficiency is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Soft, deforming bones are rickets, caused by a lack of vitamin D (which the body needs to absorb calcium) or of calcium itself. Vitamin C deficiency is scurvy, which affects gums and healing, not bone hardness.

questions.stem: Which organ is an ASSOCIATED organ of the alimentary canal — one that food does not pass through?
questions.explanation: The pancreas (like the salivary glands, liver and gall bladder) only secretes into the canal; food never enters it. The stomach, ileum and oesophagus are all parts of the canal itself.

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the correct order in which food passes through the alimentary canal?
choices: Mouth → stomach → oesophagus → small intestine → large intestine
Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine
Mouth → oesophagus → small intestine → stomach → large intestine
Mouth → stomach → small intestine → oesophagus → large intestine
questions.explanation: Food is swallowed down the oesophagus to the stomach, then passes to the small intestine (duodenum then ileum) and finally the large intestine (colon, rectum, anus). The oesophagus connects mouth to stomach — it must come between them.

choices: Taking food into the body through the mouth
Removing undigested food from the body as faeces
Breaking large food molecules down into smaller ones
Absorbed food molecules moving into cells and being used there
questions.explanation: Assimilation is what cells do with absorbed molecules — e.g. using glucose in respiration or building amino acids into the body's own proteins. Taking food in is ingestion; removing undigested food is egestion.

questions.stem: How does physical digestion help chemical digestion?
choices: It breaks food into smaller pieces, increasing the surface area for enzymes to act on
It changes starch molecules into sugars
It kills bacteria in the food
It neutralises the acid in the stomach
questions.explanation: Chewing and churning break food into smaller pieces with no chemical change; the larger surface area lets digestive enzymes work faster. Changing starch to sugars is chemical digestion, and killing microorganisms is the role of stomach acid.

questions.stem: A lion grips and tears meat from its prey. Which type of tooth is it mainly using?
questions.explanation: Canines are the pointed teeth adapted for gripping and tearing. Incisors bite and cut, while premolars and molars are broad teeth for chewing and grinding.

questions.stem: Which part of a tooth contains the nerves and blood vessels?
questions.explanation: The pulp is the soft centre of the tooth containing the nerves and blood vessels. Enamel is the hard protective outer layer, dentine lies beneath it, and cement anchors the root in the jawbone.

choices: The salivary glands and the pancreas
The gall bladder and the stomach
questions.explanation: Amylase is secreted by the salivary glands (acting in the mouth) and the pancreas (acting in the small intestine), breaking starch into simple reducing sugars. The stomach secretes protease, and the gall bladder stores bile but secretes no enzymes.

questions.stem: Which statement about lipase is correct?
choices: It breaks fats into amino acids in the stomach
It breaks starch into sugars in the mouth
It breaks fats and oils into fatty acids and glycerol in the small intestine
It breaks proteins into amino acids in the stomach
questions.explanation: Lipase is secreted by the pancreas and acts only in the small intestine, where it digests fats and oils into fatty acids and glycerol. Proteins go to amino acids via protease, and starch goes to sugars via amylase.

questions.stem: What are the functions of the hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
choices: Killing microorganisms in the food and providing an acidic pH for optimum enzyme activity
Breaking starch into sugars and lubricating the food
questions.explanation: Stomach acid has exactly two Core functions: it kills microorganisms swallowed with the food, and it provides the acidic pH in which stomach protease works best. It does not itself digest any nutrient.

questions.stem: In which part of the alimentary canal is MOST water absorbed?
questions.explanation: Most water is absorbed in the small intestine, along with the digested food molecules; only some water is absorbed later in the colon. The oesophagus absorbs nothing.

questions.stem: A patient's stomach stops producing hydrochloric acid, but all other parts of the gut work normally. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Starch can no longer be digested anywhere in the gut
Stomach protease works less effectively and more swallowed microorganisms survive
Food can no longer be ingested
Fats are no longer digested in the small intestine
questions.explanation: Without the acid, stomach enzymes lose their acidic optimum pH and microorganisms are not killed. Starch digestion (mouth and small intestine) and fat digestion (small intestine) do not depend on stomach acid, and ingestion is unaffected.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly pairs a process with its definition?
choices: Egestion — the removal of undigested food from the body as faeces
Absorption — the breakdown of food molecules by enzymes
Ingestion — the movement of nutrients from the gut into the blood
Digestion — the use of absorbed nutrients inside cells
questions.explanation: Egestion is the removal of undigested food as faeces via the anus. Enzyme breakdown is (chemical) digestion, movement into the blood is absorption, and using nutrients inside cells is assimilation — the distractors swap the definitions around.
